analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest and fees at the rate limits set by the borrower's home state.
analysis.headline: Backed by 6 senators, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a lender can charge a borrower the interest rate allowed in the state where the lender is based, not the state where the borrower lives — which is why high-cost loans are legal even in states that voted to cap them. This bill would reverse that for consumer credit: any lender charging a consumer (except on a home mortgage) could charge no more than the maximum rate allowed in the borrower's own state, and fees would count toward that cap. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who live in states with strict interest rate limits but get charged higher rates by lenders based elsewhere — for example on credit cards, payday-style loans, or installment loans. The bill would make those loans subject to the borrower's home-state cap, so a rate a state banned stays banned no matter where the lender is headquartered. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the maximum interest rate allowed in the consumer's home state to any consumer credit transaction, overriding the ability of lenders to import higher rates from the state where they are chartered or based.
Fees attached to a loan count toward the cap, closing the common workaround of layering charges on top of a nominally legal rate.
Home mortgages are excluded, so the change targets high-cost consumer credit without touching the housing finance market.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders who currently charge consumers rates above the borrower's home-state cap — chiefly credit card issuers headquartered in permissive states and high-cost installment or payday lenders, including online lenders and bank-partnership arrangements that rely on exporting a permissive state's rates. They would either cap rates in capped states or stop lending there. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: Strict rate caps do not make credit free; lenders facing a low cap in a high-risk borrower's state may simply decline to lend there, so some borrowers with poor credit could lose access to legal credit and be pushed toward informal or offshore borrowing.

The bill sets no federal fallback rate, so its effect depends entirely on each state's own usury law — a state with no meaningful cap would see no change for its residents, and the protection is only as strong as state law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in states that have chosen strict rate caps, the bill would deliver real savings and enforce the decision those states already made; the honest trade-off is that some high-risk borrowers in those states may find less credit available at any price. The bill leaves the balance to each state, which is its main design strength and its main limit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 26, 2013, with Sen. Elizabeth Warren as an original co-sponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors (4 Democrats and 1 Independent) and no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders that charge consumers rates above the borrower's home-state cap — credit card issuers based in permissive states and high-cost installment and payday-style lenders — kept their current business model intact, because no state cap now binds them outside their home state.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the chamber never took a position; the bill's only backers were 4 Democrats, 1 Independent, and its Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Payday, installment, and online high-cost consumer lenders
industries.note: These lenders' business depends on charging rates far above the caps in many borrowers' states, often by lending under the law of a permissive state or through a partner bank. Applying the borrower's home-state cap to every consumer loan would make those rates illegal in most capped states, costing them the highest-margin slice of their lending.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and out-of-state banks
industries.note: Card issuers can currently charge cardholders nationwide the rate of the state where the issuer is based, which is why issuers concentrate in states with no rate cap. Tying the cap to the borrower's state instead would force lower rates for cardholders in capped states, cutting interest and fee revenue.

industries.industry: Lenders headquartered in states without rate caps (e.g., Delaware, South Dakota)
industries.note: Their competitive advantage is exactly the rule this bill removes: the right to export their home state's unlimited rates to consumers everywhere. Losing that would shrink their national market or force lower pricing.
